sections.title: Situation
sections.prompt: What is the real decision, and what did the pilot actually show?
criteria: Says the overtime metric was the wrong measure, not proof the product failed
Separates business hours (0.4 points, not significant) from after hours (6.5 points, significant)
Derives the 2.3-day vacancy gain and its range from the 0.8-day standard error
Names the $417k already spent as sunk and irrelevant to the call

sections.title: Stakeholders
sections.prompt: Who has a stake, what does each want, and how do you bring them along?
criteria: Covers at least the VP of Engineering, leasing operations, legal and the payments migration lead
Gives the pilot sponsor a new success measure in place of overtime
Includes the engineers and what the two who stay will own
Ends with one idea that ties the stakeholders together

sections.title: Options
sections.prompt: What are the real options, and which fit 2 engineers after week 8?
criteria: Includes kill, and at least one option between kill and full scale
Shows that scaling to all 300 needs 12 engineer-months of PMS integrations the team doesn't have
Explains why extending the pilot as is buys no new information
Compares options on one table with the same criteria

sections.title: Decision and Trade-offs
sections.prompt: What do you recommend, what do you give up, and what would change your mind?
criteria: Makes one clear recommendation and says what is switched off
Names what is given up, including the PMS-B and PMS-C properties
Says the decision is reversible and how (per-property flag)
Gives a dated revisit with both an expand trigger and a kill trigger

sections.title: Economics
sections.prompt: What is the value and the cost over three years, and how sure are you?
criteria: Derives annual value from turnovers, vacancy days and daily rent ($867.5k at 120 properties)
Shows the value at the low end of the range as well as the central estimate
Derives cost per conversation from tokens and list prices, including cache reads
Shows that people, not model spend, are almost all of the cost

sections.title: Org and Ownership
sections.prompt: Who owns what once half the team has left?
criteria: Names a single accountable owner
Puts one engineer on run with a named backup and a runbook
Gives legal ownership of what counts as a fair-housing failure
Puts prompt and model changes behind the fair-housing eval

sections.title: Plan and Milestones
sections.prompt: What gets done before week 8, and where can it be stopped?
criteria: Finishes the build and rollout before the 2 engineers leave at week 8
Has a fair-housing gate with a measurable threshold before any new property goes live
Rolls out in waves rather than all at once
Includes the month-7 revisit as a milestone

sections.title: Risk and Governance
sections.prompt: What could go wrong at 120 properties, and what controls it?
criteria: Quantifies fair-housing problems a month at the new volume (about 86 unfixed)
Explains why a clean sample doesn't prove a zero rate
Puts the fair-housing control in code, not in policy or sampling alone
Addresses the lost-handoff problem with a number

sections.title: Metrics
sections.prompt: How will you know at month 7 whether to expand or kill?
criteria: Pairs each success metric with a guard metric
Uses vacancy days as the primary outcome, not share handled by AI
Names a control group for the month-7 comparison
Tracks fair-housing failures as a guard metric

sections.title: Communication
sections.prompt: What does each audience hear, and how often?
criteria: Gives a one-line message for at least four audiences
Retires the overtime target with the sponsor explicitly
Tells the payments lead the engineers arrive on time
Sets a cadence and says failed gates are reported the same day
